artworks.title: Abduction of Deianira
artworks.description: Guido Reni's Baroque masterpiece seizes the violent climax of the myth: the centaur Nessus gallops away through the surf bearing the struggling Deianira aloft, her body twisting in alarm and her drapery streaming like a banner against a stormy sky. Having been entrusted to carry her across the swollen river Evenus for hire, Nessus has instead seized the bride of Heracles and bolts for the far shore — the assault that will draw a hydra-poisoned arrow and seal both their fates. Reni dramatizes the upward spiral of bodies, the abductor's animal power set against the heroine's helpless contortion. Oil on canvas, 262 × 192 cm, now in the Louvre, Paris (INV 537).

artworks.title: Hercules Beating Nessus (Hercules and the Centaur Nessus)
artworks.description: This towering marble by the Flemish-born Mannerist Giambologna captures the moment of reckoning at the river Evenus: Heracles, planted with brute force, grips the rearing centaur Nessus and beats him down for his attempt on Deianira. The composition coils the human victor and the half-equine abductor into a single knot of strained muscle and torsion, exploiting the dramatic figura serpentinata that made Giambologna famous and inviting the viewer to circle the group. Carved in 1599, the sculpture stands in the Loggia dei Lanzi in the Piazza della Signoria, Florence, among the city's open-air gallery of heroic statuary.

artworks.title: The Abduction of Deianeira by the Centaur Nessus
artworks.description: Exhibited at the Salon of 1755, Lagrenée's polished academic canvas stages the centaur Nessus mid-flight as he carries off Deianira, her arms flung out and her gaze turned back toward the shore in mute appeal for rescue. The French painter balances classical restraint with movement: cool flesh tones and ordered drapery temper the abduction's violence into an elegant, theatrical tableau in the manner of mid-eighteenth-century history painting. The episode is the pivot of Heracles' downfall, for Nessus's dying gift of poisoned blood will later destroy the hero. Oil on canvas, 157 × 185 cm, Musée du Louvre, Paris (INV 5552).

artworks.title: Nessus and Deianira (Neso y Deyanira)
artworks.description: Painted in 1888 by the Spanish artist Enrique Simonet during his formative years in Rome, this academic canvas revisits the abduction at the Evenus: the centaur Nessus surges forward carrying Deianira, her pale form set against his dark equine body in a study of contrasting flesh, motion, and resistance. Simonet renders the mythological subject with the careful anatomical drawing and dramatic naturalism prized in late nineteenth-century academic training. Oil on canvas, 116 × 151 cm; the work is associated with the collection of the Universidad Complutense de Madrid.
